note: Hebrew tachash is uncertain (dugong/sea-cow, a dyed leather, or a fine leather from an Egyptian loanword); badgers are unlikely. Recurs in 4:8-14, 4:25. Context: a fine leather (medium confidence). As Exod 39:34: tachash is uncertain but denotes a valued material (Ezek 16:10), not a badger's pelt. 'Fine leather' (NRSV, NET; NIV 'durable leather') commits least to a species. Other possible meanings: (1) sea-cow/dugong or dolphin/porpoise skins — NJPS 'dolphin skins', NASB95 'porpoise skins', NIV 1984 'sea cows'; (2) violet/blue-dyed skins — LXX hyakinthina, Vulgate ianthina; (3) goatskins — ESV; (4) 'badgers' skins' — KJV, from a Talmudic identification of tachash as an animal.

mine: the jugs for the drink offering
note: Hebrew qesot hannesek are pitchers or jars "of the libation", vessels for pouring, not lids.
Hebrew mot is a pole-frame or litter for carrying, not a single bar.
Hebrew minchat hatamid is the continual grain offering; "meat" meant food in 1611 and now misleads.

kjv: to see when the holy things are covered
mine: to look at the holy things even for a moment
note: Hebrew kevalla' is literally "as a swallowing", most likely an idiom for "an instant" (like "a gulp"); the KJV took it as the covering ("swallowing up") of the objects. Context: even for a moment (medium confidence). 4:15-19 forbid the Kohathites to touch or see the holy things; kevalla' 'as a swallowing' is best taken as an idiom for an instant (cf. Job 7:19 'till I swallow my spit'), as ESV, NIV, NASB, NRSV and CSB render. The Targum and Vulgate instead relate it to the wrapping of the objects. Other possible meanings: (1) 'when the holy things are covered/wrapped' (bala' 'swallow up, envelop') — Targum Onkelos, Vulgate, Rashi, KJV; (2) 'witness the dismantling of the sanctuary' (bala' 'take down') — NJPS; (3) 'suddenly' — LXX exapina.
